lead.topic: Population genetics: bottlenecks, genetic load and inbreeding
lead.headline: A bottleneck does not guarantee genetic recovery
lead.deck: New theory separates the loss of inbreeding depression from the harder recovery of population fitness.
paragraphs: When a population suddenly shrinks, relatives are more likely to inherit the same variants, including harmful recessive mutations. These mutations can reduce survival or reproduction when both copies are harmful. Conservation geneticists therefore ask: does increased homozygosity expose damaging variants to selection strongly enough to remove them, and can average fitness eventually recover? Eugenio López-Cortegano and Brian Charlesworth address those questions with population genetic theory in Genetics. They consider a small, randomly mating population founded from a much larger population at mutation-selection-drift equilibrium, the long-term balance of mutation, selection and chance.

The authors combine computer simulations with approximate mathematical predictions for changes after the bottleneck. Their results show that purging can accelerate the loss of inbreeding depression, the extra fitness cost of mating between relatives. But an actual recovery in mean fitness requires mutations to be sufficiently recessive and selection to be strong enough relative to drift. Weakly harmful mutations instead produce declines in fitness and inbreeding depression broadly comparable to those expected from rising homozygosity under a neutral model, at least over the short periods studied. Reduced inbreeding depression, therefore, is not proof that a population has become genetically healthy. This is a theoretical result, not evidence that bottlenecked wild populations inevitably rebound.
lead.push: Extend the framework to populations whose sizes rebound after a crash, with linked loci and nonrandom mating. Across simulations, ask whether the decline of inbreeding depression predicts absolute fitness recovery or merely loss of segregating variation. Then test these divergent forecasts against pedigreed conservation populations with multigenerational survival and reproductive data.

people.name: Eugenio López-Cortegano
people.bio: Eugenio López-Cortegano is a statistical geneticist whose research spans mutational load, genetic purging, conservation genetics and population breeding. The new paper lists affiliations with the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Ecology and Evolution and Aviagen Ltd. He earned a doctorate in population genetics at the Complutense University of Madrid in 2017.

people.name: Brian Charlesworth
people.bio: Brian Charlesworth is a Senior Honorary Professorial Fellow at the University of Edinburgh and a leading population geneticist. After earning a doctorate in genetics at Cambridge in 1969, he did postdoctoral research with Richard Lewontin at the University of Chicago. His work addresses selection, recombination, drift and genome evolution.

slot2.headline: The brain's regions differ in how they combine information
slot2.cite: Ruff et al., Nature Neuroscience (10 Nov 2026). Research article.
slot2.body: Two regions of the brain may carry the same information but use it differently. Ruff and colleagues recorded neuronal populations in two rhesus monkeys judging the direction of moving dots while considering potential juice rewards. Visual area MT represented motion and reward largely separately; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex combined them in overlapping population patterns. A recurrent neural network generated predictions for stimulation experiments. Stimulating MT shifted judgments toward the represented motion direction, while stimulation of prefrontal cortex more often produced all-or-none, winner-take-all choices. Reading information from neural activity, the authors argue, does not establish what computation that tissue performs.

slot3.headline: Tangled DNA makes a restless liquid beat in unison
slot3.cite: Levanon et al., Nature Physics (09 Nov 2026). Research article.
slot3.body: Can a liquid of randomly swirling molecular motors organize itself into a coordinated rhythm? In a Nature Physics experiment, researchers combined microtubules and kinesin motors with long strands of DNA. Initially, the motors drove irregular fluid motion. The motion stretched and tangled the DNA, building an elastic network that then fed back on the flow. Above a threshold DNA length, the mixture developed synchronized vortices spanning roughly two millimeters and reversing on timescales of tens of minutes. Shorter DNA strands did not produce stable oscillations. The work reveals mechanical self-organization without a chemical timing circuit, suggesting design principles for responsive soft materials.
